title: RBI Raises Investment Limits for NRIs and OCIs in Indian Equities
excerpt: The Reserve Bank of India will allow NRIs, OCIs and all overseas individuals to hold larger stakes in listed Indian companies without registering as foreign portfolio investors, in a broader push to attract diaspora capital.
body:
• Individual NRI/OCI investment cap in listed companies already raised from 5% to 10% post-Budget 2026; RBI signals further increases ahead
  • Combined overseas investor limit more than doubled from 10% to 24%, with the facility extended to all Persons Resident Outside India
  • Move is part of a wider capital-attraction strategy that includes expanded bond access and a temporary FCNR deposit window that has already drawn $10 billion

The Reserve Bank of India has announced it will further raise the limits on how much Non-Resident Indians, Overseas Citizens of India and other overseas individuals can invest in listed Indian companies without registering as Foreign Portfolio Investors with SEBI, Livemint reported.

The move is part of a sweeping package of measures designed to channel more overseas capital into Indian financial markets at a time when the rupee faces renewed pressure from surging oil prices and geopolitical uncertainty.

What Changed

Following Budget 2026, the maximum stake an individual NRI, OCI or eligible overseas investor can hold in a listed company was already raised from 5% to 10% of its paid-up equity capital. The combined limit for all such investors was more than doubled, from 10% to 24%.

These thresholds determine how much overseas individuals can invest through the regular NRI investment framework — a far simpler route than the FPI regime, which requires registration, compliance and ongoing reporting obligations.

The RBI has now signalled that both the individual and aggregate limits will be increased further, though the revised thresholds have not yet been disclosed. The facility will also be extended to all individual Persons Resident Outside India, widening the pool of eligible investors beyond NRIs and OCIs.

Why It Matters for the Diaspora

For most retail NRI investors, the current limits are more than adequate. But for wealthy individuals, family offices and investors looking to build concentrated positions in Indian companies, the distinction between the NRI route and the FPI route carries real weight.

By raising the non-FPI investment ceiling, the RBI is reducing regulatory friction for overseas investors who want greater exposure to Indian equities. In practical terms, a diaspora investor in the US, UK or Singapore can now deploy significantly more capital into a single Indian stock without triggering the heavier compliance requirements of FPI registration.

Part of a Bigger Push

The NRI investment relaxation sits alongside several other measures aimed at attracting foreign capital. The RBI has expanded the Fully Accessible Route for government securities by including all new issuances of 15-year, 30-year and 40-year bonds. It has also removed certain concentration and short-term investment restrictions for foreign portfolio investors in government securities, according to Livemint.

Separately, the RBI introduced temporary incentives for external commercial borrowings and fresh 3-5 year FCNR(B) deposits until September 30, 2026. Under this window, banks can offer higher interest rates on foreign currency deposits from NRIs and Persons of Indian Origin.

The FCNR initiative has already drawn roughly $10 billion in inflows, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter. Economists and bankers estimate the programme could ultimately attract between $30 billion and $60 billion in foreign-currency deposits. ICAI Singapore Chapter Chairman Sanjay Gattani told PTI the broader potential could reach $70-80 billion.

The Rupee Factor

The timing is deliberate. The rupee weakened past 96 per dollar this week, less than 1% from its all-time low of 96.96, under pressure from rising oil prices linked to the Iran conflict. The FCNR deposits and broader capital-attraction measures are designed to shore up India's foreign exchange reserves and support the currency.

For NRI investors, the combination of higher investment limits and attractive deposit rates creates a window of opportunity — though the final numbers on how far the equity caps will rise remain to be seen.
